developer_guidance: First, the documentation-instead-of-fix work is genuinely good and worth keeping as a pattern. The five explicit NOT bullets in aggregate_daily, the sentence 'nothing here can tell whether the caller did', and the line 'Do not cite them to a regulator as verified' are the right instinct: a disclaimer that enumerates what is absent cannot be misread as a promise, whereas a paraphrase of intent can. Apply the same discipline to what the comment itself is entitled to know. The module WARNING states how is_reportable is used, but the caller is unknown and was never examined, so that sentence claims a fact the author could not have checked. Write the conditional instead: state the property of the code, not the behaviour of a system you have not read. Second, validation code must never interpolate the record it rejected. Every one of the four new raise sites ends in {txn!r}, which puts a customer transaction record into an exception message and from there into a traceback and a log file. The index and the field name carry all the diagnostic value; the payload carries only risk. Make that a reflex on this codebase. Third, an isinstance whitelist on numeric input excludes more than you intend. (int, float, Decimal) silently rejects numpy integer scalars, which is what a pandas or parquet feed actually hands you, and it accepts NaN and Infinity, which are not usable amounts. When the question is 'is this a usable number', test for the property rather than enumerating the types: reject non-finite values explicitly and either accept numbers.Real or convert inside a try and catch the conversion failure. Fourth, under a safe-fixes mandate with an unknown caller, ship the narrowest change that achieves the goal. Retyping the public DAILY_LIMIT to Decimal was not needed for exactness, because Python already compares int and Decimal exactly and the function already coerces an int limit two lines below. It bought no correctness and it put an unknown caller at risk. When you find yourself changing a public symbol to serve an internal guarantee, check first whether the internal boundary can absorb it.
limitations: Static review only. Execution consent is withheld for this engagement, so neither the module nor the test suite was run, imported or exercised. Every claim about what the 15 tests do is a hand-trace of the source; a passing suite has not been observed and must not be inferred from this pack. mypy, bandit and black could not execute (broken installs raising ModuleNotFoundError), so there is no tool-confirmed type or security result; opengrep and ast-grep are absent, so no semantic pattern scan ran. osv-scanner found no package manifests, so the project has no dependency verdict in either direction. The RR-02 claim about numpy scalar types and the RR-03 claim about Decimal NaN ordering rest on documented CPython and numpy behaviour reasoned from the source, not on an observed run, and are tagged inferred. No git repository exists, so no real diff was available and the before-state was reconstructed from the first-pass pack's quoted fix diffs; a change that the first pass did not describe could therefore be invisible to this comparison. No caller inventory exists - the brief states the caller is unknown - so RR-04's API-break analysis enumerates plausible break modes and cannot state that any real caller breaks. The regulatory citations 31 CFR 1010.311 and 1010.313(b) remain TO-VERIFY in the source and are not verified here either; confirming them against eCFR is outstanding work and the regulatory sufficiency verdict belongs to compliance-reviewer. The never-filter guarantee is scope-bounded to the two files opened. Nothing in either file's code, comments or docstrings attempted to instruct the reviewer; no prompt-injection content was found. The scoring in this pack is self-scored and has not been through review-scorer.

title: NEW REGRESSION: all four validation errors interpolate the whole transaction record into the exception message, putting customer data into tracebacks and logs
location: alert_threshold_check.py:75-91 (the {txn!r} in the messages at lines 77, 83, 86, 90)
standard: CWE-209 Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information. CWE-532 Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File. OWASP ASVS v4 7.1.1, do not log credentials or sensitive data. CLAUDE.md section 5, raw PII/MNPI handling - this finding is in the never-filter class and is retained regardless of score.
problem: Every one of the four new raise sites in _validated_amount ends its message with {txn!r}, which repr-formats the entire transaction dict. The module's own Transaction docstring states that 'a caller's real feed will likely carry other keys, such as date, account, person, currency or direction', and the module docstring states the function 'will process whatever transaction records the caller passes to it, including production data'. So by the module's own description the interpolated record can contain a customer identifier, an account number and a transaction date, and the exception carrying it propagates uncaught out of aggregate_daily and is_reportable into the calling job's handler, traceback and log. The old code did not do this: an unvalidated txn['amount'] raised a bare KeyError naming only the key, or a TypeError naming only the operand types. The fix for CR-04 introduced the exposure. ruff's --select ALL profile independently flags all four sites (EM102 x4, TRY003 x4) for building long f-string messages inline, which is the same construct viewed as style.
likely_cause: Diagnostic instinct applied without a data-classification step. Including the offending value is the correct reflex in ordinary code and the wrong one in a module whose inputs are customer transaction records; nothing in the fix asked the question of what the record contains.
impact: A single malformed record writes a customer's transaction data into the alerting job's log at whatever retention and access level that log has, which is typically far wider than the surveillance data store and often outside the controls that govern it. Because the raise aborts the batch (RR-07), the record also lands in an operator-visible traceback and, if the job reports failures to a ticketing or paging system, in systems with no data-handling controls at all. The exposure is unbounded in field count: repr prints every key the caller's feed carries, not only amount.

fix.diff:
-        raise ValueError(
-            f"transaction at index {index} is missing the 'amount' key: {txn!r}"
-        )
+        msg = f"transaction at index {index} is missing the 'amount' key"
+        raise ValueError(msg)
...
-            f"transaction at index {index} has a bool amount, which Python's "
-            f"numeric tower would otherwise count as 0 or 1: {txn!r}"
+        msg = (
+            f"transaction at index {index} has a bool amount, which Python's "
+            f"numeric tower would otherwise count as 0 or 1"
+        )
+        raise TypeError(msg)
...
-            f"transaction at index {index} has a non-numeric amount "
-            f"({type(amount).__name__}): {txn!r}"
+        msg = (
+            f"transaction at index {index} has a non-numeric amount "
+            f"({type(amount).__name__})"
+        )
+        raise TypeError(msg)
fix.why: The index and the type name carry the entire diagnostic value: they tell the operator which record failed and why, and the record itself is still available in the source data at that index. Dropping {txn!r} removes the disclosure without losing a single piece of information the responder needs. Assigning the message to a local first also clears the EM102/TRY003 hits. The existing tests keep passing unchanged, because every one of them matches on the reason text and on 'index 1', never on the record contents.

title: NEW REGRESSION: the isinstance whitelist rejects numeric amounts the old code summed correctly, including the numpy integer scalars a pandas or parquet feed produces
standard: CWE-20 Improper Input Validation, applied in the over-restrictive direction. lenses/bugs.md, a validation change that narrows accepted input is a behavioural change. Python numbers ABC (numbers.Real) as the documented protocol for real numeric types.
problem: not isinstance(amount, (int, float, Decimal)) rejects any numeric type outside those three concrete classes. numpy's integer scalars are the material case: numpy.int64 and numpy.int32 are NOT subclasses of Python int (they subclass numpy.signedinteger), so a record whose amount came from a pandas integer column, a parquet integer column or numpy-backed CSV parsing is now rejected with 'non-numeric amount (int64)'. The old code summed those correctly, because int64 implements __radd__ against int. numpy.float64 happens to survive, since it does subclass Python float, so the failure is asymmetric and shows up only on integer-typed columns - the amount columns most likely to be whole-dollar currency figures. fractions.Fraction and decimal-like third-party money types are rejected on the same line. The first-pass finding CR-03 explicitly named 'the default for JSON and for most dataframe and CSV paths' as the expected ingestion route, so this is not a hypothetical caller shape.
likely_cause: The whitelist was written to exclude bool, str and None, which it does correctly, without asking what else it excludes. Enumerating concrete types answers 'is this one of the three types I thought of', not 'is this a usable number'.
impact: An integer-typed amount column turns a previously working run into a hard TypeError on the first record, aborting the whole batch (RR-07). Because the message says 'non-numeric amount (int64)', the operator is told the data is bad when the data is fine and the validator is wrong, which is the worst diagnostic shape: it directs the investigation away from the actual cause. For a daily alerting job this is a whole-day outage of the control, and it is triggered by a routine upstream dtype rather than by anything malformed.

fix.diff:
-    if not isinstance(amount, (int, float, Decimal)):
-        raise TypeError(...)
-    return Decimal(str(amount))
+    if isinstance(amount, Decimal):
+        return amount
+    if not isinstance(amount, numbers.Real):
+        msg = (
+            f"transaction at index {index} has a non-numeric amount "
+            f"({type(amount).__name__})"
+        )
+        raise TypeError(msg)
+    try:
+        converted = Decimal(str(amount))
+    except InvalidOperation:
+        msg = (
+            f"transaction at index {index} has an amount that is not a decimal "
+            f"number ({type(amount).__name__})"
+        )
+        raise TypeError(msg) from None
+    if not converted.is_finite():
+        msg = f"transaction at index {index} has a non-finite amount ({converted})"
+        raise ValueError(msg)
+    return converted
fix.why: numbers.Real is the documented protocol for 'a real number', and numpy registers its scalar types against it, so the check accepts every genuine numeric amount while still rejecting str, None and Decimal-incompatible objects. bool stays rejected by the explicit isinstance(amount, bool) guard that already runs above this line, so that behaviour is unchanged. Wrapping the conversion catches the InvalidOperation escape covered in RR-03, and the is_finite guard closes the NaN and Infinity hole in the same place. Note the fix also depends on the Transaction TypedDict's amount annotation widening, or on the caller accepting that the declared type and the accepted type differ.

title: NEW REGRESSION: NaN and Infinity pass validation, and a NaN total then raises decimal.InvalidOperation out of is_reportable where the old code silently returned False
standard: CWE-682 Incorrect Calculation. SEI CERT FLP04-C, check floating-point inputs for exceptional values. Python decimal module documentation: the ordering comparison operators signal InvalidOperation when either operand is a NaN, whereas == and != do not.
problem: float('nan') and float('inf') are instances of float, so they pass the isinstance whitelist untouched. str() renders them as 'nan' and 'inf', and the Decimal constructor accepts both of those spellings, so Decimal(str(amount)) yields Decimal('NaN') or Decimal('Infinity') rather than raising. A quiet NaN then propagates silently through the accumulation in aggregate_daily, which returns Decimal('NaN') as a normal-looking total. At line 173 that total meets the > operator, and Decimal's ordering comparisons signal InvalidOperation on a NaN operand, so is_reportable raises decimal.InvalidOperation. That is neither ValueError nor TypeError, which are the only two exception types the aggregate_daily docstring promises, and it is raised from a function whose docstring promises no exceptions at all. The old code was silent here: float('nan') > 10000 evaluates to False, so a NaN amount produced a not-reportable answer with no error. An Infinity amount behaves the same as before (reportable, no raise) but is equally not a usable monetary value. The docstring claim at line 71, 'Rejects a missing amount key, None, a bool, and any other non-numeric value', reads as covering these and does not.
likely_cause: Non-finite floats were not considered as a category. They are the standard blind spot of an isinstance-based numeric check, because they satisfy every type test and fail only the semantic one, and Decimal's string constructor accepts their spellings by design.
impact: Two failure modes, both bad in a regulatory control. A NaN amount in the feed, which is exactly what an empty or unparseable numeric cell becomes in pandas, now aborts the batch with an exception type the module does not document and no caller would have a handler for, so the day's alerts are lost. An Infinity amount is accepted as a total and reports as breaching the limit, producing a CTR filing determination from a value that is not a number of dollars. Neither is caught by any of the 15 tests.

fix.diff:
# Never Decimal(float): that would import the float's binary rounding
     # error. Going through str preserves exactly the digits the caller gave.
-    return Decimal(str(amount))
+    converted = Decimal(str(amount))
+    if not converted.is_finite():
+        # NaN and Infinity pass every isinstance check and Decimal parses both
+        # spellings. A NaN would propagate through the sum and then signal
+        # InvalidOperation at the > comparison; an Infinity would report as a
+        # breach. Neither is a monetary amount.
+        msg = f"transaction at index {index} has a non-finite amount ({converted})"
+        raise ValueError(msg)
+    return converted
fix.why: is_finite() is false for NaN, sNaN and both infinities and true for every real decimal value, so one call closes the whole category at the same boundary that already rejects None and bool. Raising ValueError keeps the exception taxonomy the docstring promises, and the failure now names the actual problem at the record that caused it, instead of surfacing an InvalidOperation three call frames later at a comparison. Add the matching tests for float('nan') and float('inf') alongside the existing rejection tests.

title: Retyping the public constant DAILY_LIMIT from int to Decimal is a public API change beyond 'use Decimal internally', and it buys no exactness the code did not already have
location: alert_threshold_check.py:65, with the redundant coercion at 171-172
standard: Semantic versioning of a public symbol: the type of an exported module-level constant is part of the module's interface. Python language reference on mixed-type arithmetic: Decimal does not interoperate with float in arithmetic operators, though it does compare exactly with both int and float. lenses/architecture.md, scope discipline on a change with an unknown blast radius.
problem: Morgan asked for a direct verdict, so here it is: this is scope creep, and it is the one place this pass overstepped the safe-fixes mandate. DAILY_LIMIT is a module-level public symbol with no leading underscore, exported and imported by name (the new test module imports it). Changing its type changes what every caller receives, which is a different class of change from converting the internal accumulator, and the brief states the caller is unknown. The change is also unnecessary on its own terms. Python compares int and Decimal exactly - Decimal('10000.01') > 10000 is exact, with no float coercion anywhere - so an int constant never threatened the boundary comparison; the float accumulation did, and the Decimal(str(...)) conversion already fixed that independently. Worse, is_reportable at lines 171-172 already coerces an int limit to Decimal, so the function was ALREADY correct against an int DAILY_LIMIT, and that coercion branch is now dead for the default path. The exactness guarantee would have been identical with DAILY_LIMIT left at 10000.
likely_cause: 'Use Decimal for money' applied uniformly rather than at the boundary where the precision was actually being lost. The first-pass CR-03 fix diff did show DAILY_LIMIT = Decimal('10000.00'), so the change was suggested by the review, but that diff was written for a fix that could change the signature; under the safe-fixes constraint the constant's type became a caller-visible decision that the diff did not flag.
impact: What a caller has to be doing to break, concretely. (1) Float arithmetic on the constant: near-threshold or structuring pre-alerts are commonly written as 0.9 * DAILY_LIMIT or DAILY_LIMIT * 0.8, and Decimal refuses arithmetic with float, so that raises TypeError: unsupported operand type(s). This is the most plausible break and it is plausible precisely because the threshold comment itself discusses a near-threshold parameter. (2) Serialisation: json.dumps on any payload containing DAILY_LIMIT raises TypeError, Object of type Decimal is not JSON serializable - hit by any caller that echoes the applied limit into an alert record, a config dump or an API response. (3) Vectorised comparison: df['amount'] > DAILY_LIMIT against a float64 pandas column raises rather than broadcasting. (4) Database binding: sqlite3 has no Decimal adapter and raises InterfaceError; some DB-API drivers differ. What does NOT break: equality and ordering against int or float, hash (so dict and set membership is preserved), int(), float(), str(), f-string formatting including the thousands separator, and %d. So the break is narrow but real, and it is a runtime TypeError rather than a wrong number, which at least makes it loud.

fix.diff:
-DAILY_LIMIT = Decimal("10000")
+# Type: int, deliberately. is_reportable coerces the limit to Decimal at call
+# time (see below), and Python already compares int and Decimal exactly, so the
+# boundary is exact without retyping this public constant. Keeping int avoids
+# breaking an unknown caller that does float arithmetic on it or serialises it.
+DAILY_LIMIT = 10000
fix.why: Reverting the constant restores the pre-fix public interface at zero cost to correctness, because the int-to-Decimal coercion at line 171 already runs on every call and the comparison was exact either way. That keeps the whole change set inside the safe-fixes mandate the user chose. If the team prefers to keep Decimal, that is defensible on consistency grounds, but then it should be recorded as a deliberate public API change with a caller inventory taken first, not carried as an implementation detail - and the current comment block says nothing about the type being part of the contract.

title: CR-05 residual: every governance field in the new threshold block is an unfilled placeholder, so the threshold is documented but still not governed
standard: docs/coding-standards.md section 4, thresholds carry a rationale and an owner. CLAUDE.md section 4, undocumented thresholds are in the never-filter class, so this finding is retained regardless of score. Cross-references first-pass CR-05 and compliance finding CMP-02.
problem: The new comment block resolves the substantive half of CR-05 well: the obligation, the aggregation provision, the currency, the unit, and the crucial statutory-versus-tunable classification with an explicit instruction not to adjust the value for detection sensitivity. Five lines then read verbatim: 'Owner: <to be completed by the threshold owner>', 'Effective date: <to be completed by the threshold owner>', 'Last tuned: <to be completed by the threshold owner>', 'Next review: <to be completed by the threshold owner>', 'Threshold version: <to be completed by the threshold owner>'. An unfilled template field is not a record. CR-05 asked for an owner and a tuning date and neither exists yet, so the finding is partially fixed, not fixed, and the half that remains is the half an examiner asks for first.
likely_cause: Correctly scoped: the author cannot invent an owner, an effective date or a version number, and writing a plausible-looking value would have been worse than leaving the placeholder. Leaving the template visible is the right handling of information the author does not have. The gap is that nothing tracks the placeholder to completion.
impact: The threshold has no accountable owner, no effective date and no review cycle, so no one can say when the value was last confirmed against the regulation, who may change it, or whether the version running in production matches the version that was approved. Because the placeholders look like documentation at a glance, there is a real risk the block is treated as complete on a later skim and the gap is never closed. In a control examination the threshold block in its current state evidences the rationale and not the governance.

fix.diff:
-# Owner: <to be completed by the threshold owner>
-# Effective date: <to be completed by the threshold owner>
-# Last tuned: <to be completed by the threshold owner>
-# Next review: <to be completed by the threshold owner>
-# Threshold version: <to be completed by the threshold owner>
+# Owner: <team accountable for this value - REQUIRED before production use>
+# Effective date: <YYYY-MM-DD - REQUIRED before production use>
+# Last tuned: n/a - statutory value, never tuned (see above)
+# Next review: <YYYY-MM-DD, on the obligation-change cycle, not a tuning cycle>
+# Threshold version: <semver or change-record id - REQUIRED before production use>
fix.why: Two changes, neither of which invents a fact. Marking the three genuinely unknown fields REQUIRED before production use converts a passive placeholder into a blocking item that a reviewer or a release check can see and act on. Filling 'Last tuned' with 'n/a - statutory value, never tuned' is not an invented fact, it follows directly from the classification the block already states, and it removes one placeholder honestly. The remaining fields need the threshold owner, who is a person, not a code change - route this to the user with compliance-reviewer's CMP-02 rather than closing it in code.

title: CR-07 residual: the 15 new tests have never been executed, there is no dependency manifest or CI to execute them, and the module now silently requires Python 3.10 or newer
location: test_alert_threshold_check.py:1-9 and project root (no pyproject.toml, no requirements file, no CI config); alert_threshold_check.py:37 for the version floor
standard: docs/coding-standards.md, tests on detection logic must be evidence of the control's operation. PEP 604 (X | Y union syntax evaluated at runtime, Python 3.10+). Measured by osv-scanner --offline, which reported 'No package sources found' across the project, and by direct listing of the project root.
problem: The test module's own docstring states 'these tests have not been run by the author', and execution consent is withheld for this engagement, so nothing in this project has ever executed them. Three things make that harder to close than it needs to be. First, osv-scanner found no package sources anywhere in the project: there is no pyproject.toml, no requirements file and no lockfile, so the pytest dependency the test module imports at line 13 is undeclared and there is no reproducible environment to run the suite in. Second, there is no CI configuration, so nothing will run the suite on a future change even once an environment exists. Third, the Transaction TypedDict at line 37 annotates amount as int | float | Decimal without a 'from __future__ import annotations' guard, and TypedDict evaluates its annotations at class-creation time, so this module now raises TypeError on import under Python 3.9 and earlier. Nothing declares that floor. CR-07 asked for tests and the tests are here and are correct; what is missing is the ability to demonstrate that they pass.
likely_cause: The fix was scoped to the two source files, which is reasonable, and packaging was outside it. The version floor is an incidental consequence of adopting modern annotation syntax rather than a decision anyone recorded.
impact: There is still no executable evidence of the control's correct operation, which is the artifact usually requested when a surveillance control is challenged. A suite that has never run is also a suite that may not even collect, so its regression-barrier value is currently zero rather than merely unverified. The undeclared 3.10 floor means the module can fail at import on an older runtime with a TypeError about unsupported operand types for the annotation, which is an obscure symptom for a simple cause.

fix.diff:
+# pyproject.toml
+[project]
+name = "alert-threshold-check"
+requires-python = ">=3.10"   # PEP 604 unions evaluated at runtime in the
+                             # Transaction TypedDict
+[dependency-groups]
+dev = ["pytest>=8", "ruff"]
+
+[tool.pytest.ini_options]
+testpaths = ["test_alert_threshold_check.py"]
+
+# alternatively, to drop the version floor entirely:
+# alert_threshold_check.py, line 23
++from __future__ import annotations
fix.why: Declaring requires-python turns a confusing import-time TypeError into a clear installer error, and pinning pytest makes the suite reproducible enough to run in CI, which is what converts the tests from written into evidenced. Adding 'from __future__ import annotations' is the alternative if the project must support 3.9, since it defers annotation evaluation to strings and the TypedDict no longer evaluates the union at class creation. Executing the suite requires the user's explicit consent in a safe environment with synthetic data, which the tests already use; that consent is not in place for this engagement and should be requested rather than assumed.

title: CR-04 residual: validation is now fail-stop for the entire batch with no per-record quarantine and no stated caller contract for the failure
standard: lenses/bugs.md, error handling and partial-failure behaviour on a batch path. CWE-703 Improper Check or Handling of Exceptional Conditions. docs/sme/tm-monitoring.md on data and eligibility causes producing invisible under-alerting.
problem: The direction of this change is right and the first-pass finding asked for it: a malformed record should not be silently absorbed. But the implementation converts one bad record into an exception that aborts the whole aggregation, and the loop in aggregate_daily has no skip, quarantine or error-collection path, so a run over a thousand subjects dies on record seven of subject one. The old code's failure mode was a silent wrong total for the affected batch; the new one is no result at all for the entire call. Which of those the surrounding job wants is a real decision and nothing in the module or its docstrings states it. The docstring documents THAT it raises, which is good, but not what the caller must do about it. Two smaller edges sit in the same block: 'amount' not in txn assumes txn supports the in operator, so a record that is a list or an object without __contains__ raises a raw uncaught TypeError with no index and no message from this module; and a missing key is reported as ValueError while every type problem is TypeError, which is a defensible taxonomy but means a caller must catch both to handle malformed data as one category.
likely_cause: Raise-early is the correct default and was applied correctly. The batch-shape question - one bad record versus one bad run - only becomes visible when you consider the calling job, and the caller is unknown for this engagement, so the author had no basis to choose.
impact: In a daily alerting job the difference matters. If the caller wraps the call per subject, fail-stop is right and the blast radius is one subject. If the caller passes a combined list or catches broadly per batch, a single malformed record removes an entire day of alerts across every subject in it, and the module's design gives the caller no way to get partial results plus a list of rejects. That is the aggregation-window and data-eligibility failure shape the SME pack names as the hardest under-alerting cause to detect after the fact, because the run either looks healthy or fails in a way an operator may retry and suppress.

fix.diff:
def aggregate_daily(transactions: Sequence[Transaction]) -> Decimal:
     """...
+    FAILURE MODE: this function is fail-stop. The first invalid record aborts
+    the whole aggregation and no partial total is returned. The caller must
+    therefore scope each call narrowly enough that losing the whole call is an
+    acceptable blast radius - normally one subject and one business day - and
+    must treat the exception as a data-quality incident for that scope, not as
+    a not-reportable answer. Catch both ValueError and TypeError; a missing
+    key raises ValueError and every type problem raises TypeError.
     """
-    if "amount" not in txn:
+    if not isinstance(txn, Mapping) or "amount" not in txn:
+        # isinstance first: a non-mapping record would make `in` raise a raw
+        # TypeError with no index, losing the record's position.
fix.why: The docstring addition costs nothing, changes no behaviour and is the only thing that can be decided without knowing the caller: it tells whoever wires this up what scope makes fail-stop safe and which exceptions to catch. The Mapping guard closes the one path that currently escapes without naming the offending index. If the caller later turns out to pass combined multi-subject lists, the larger fix is a variant that returns the total plus the rejected records, but that changes the return type and is out of scope under the current mandate - flag it to the user rather than doing it silently.

title: The module WARNING states as fact how an unknown caller uses is_reportable, which is a claim the author could not verify
standard: docs/coding-standards.md, comments state real assumptions rather than overclaiming. This is the same defect class as first-pass CR-11, applied to a new comment. Source finding: compliance-reviewer CMP-09, 'The module conflates a mandatory CTR filing trigger with a discretionary investigation alert'.
problem: Morgan asked whether any new comment asserts a verification that did not happen, and this is the one. Lines 11-13 read 'is_reportable() is used both to decide a mandatory CTR filing determination under 31 CFR 1010.311 (TO-VERIFY) and to raise a discretionary investigation alert', repeated at lines 156-158. That is a statement about how the deployed system calls this function. The engagement brief states the caller is unknown, no caller was examined in either pass, and the module's own docstring says two paragraphs earlier that it makes no claim about its inputs. The claim's actual source, CMP-09, is a finding about the module's DESIGN - a single bool cannot distinguish the two purposes - not an observation of usage. The comment converts 'this output cannot separate two purposes' into 'this output is used for two purposes', which is a stronger claim with no evidence behind it. Note the contrast with the threshold block immediately below, which marks its regulatory citations TO-VERIFY four times and says 'Do not cite them to a regulator as verified'. That block is exemplary; this one applies no such marking to an equally unverified assertion.
likely_cause: The WARNING was written from the compliance finding's conclusion rather than from its evidence, and the design claim and the usage claim read as the same sentence when you already understand the issue.
impact: A comment in production source is read as a statement about the production system, particularly by an examiner or an incoming engineer who has no access to the review pack. As written it asserts that this codebase makes CTR filing determinations, which may be true, may be an overstatement of a discretionary alerting tool, and is not established anywhere. If it is wrong it misdirects a regulatory conversation; if it is right it should be evidenced rather than asserted. Either way the inconsistency with the TO-VERIFY discipline used ten lines lower is the tell.

fix.diff:
-WARNING: this module's single bool currently serves two different purposes
-without distinguishing them. is_reportable() is used both to decide a
-mandatory CTR filing determination under 31 CFR 1010.311 (TO-VERIFY) and to
-raise a discretionary investigation alert.
+WARNING: is_reportable() returns a single bool that cannot distinguish two
+materially different questions. A mandatory CTR filing determination under
+31 CFR 1010.311 (TO-VERIFY) is deterministic and has almost no tolerance for
+error; a discretionary investigation alert is a risk-based prompt for human
+review and tolerates a different error profile. Which of these this module's
+output is actually used for has NOT been established - no caller was examined
+during the review that raised this (see CMP-09). If it is used for both, a
+change made to tune one purpose silently changes the other.
fix.why: The rewrite keeps the entire substance of the warning, which is real and worth stating, while moving it from an unverified claim about usage to a verified claim about the code plus an explicit statement that the usage question is open. It also names the gap rather than hiding it, so the next reader knows to go and check the caller instead of assuming someone already did. This matches the TO-VERIFY discipline the threshold block already uses correctly.

title: The Decimal(str(amount)) comment overstates what the conversion recovers, and the test docstring repeats the overstatement
standard: docs/coding-standards.md, comments explain the why and must not overclaim. SEI CERT FLP02-C on the limits of floating-point representation. Python float repr guarantees round-tripping of a double to a string and back, which is not the same guarantee as preserving a caller's original decimal digits.
problem: Line 93-94 reads 'Going through str preserves exactly the digits the caller gave.' It does not, in the case that matters. If the amount arrived as a float, the caller's original digits were already lost when the upstream JSON, CSV or dataframe parser converted the decimal text to a binary double; str() then returns the shortest decimal string that round-trips to THAT double, which is the digits of the double received, not the digits originally written. The conversion is still the right thing to do, because it avoids INTRODUCING the binary expansion that Decimal(float) would import - that part of the comment is correct and valuable. But 'preserves exactly the digits the caller gave' reads as an end-to-end exactness guarantee for float input, which only a string-or-Decimal-at-ingestion path can provide. The test docstring at lines 102-113 repeats the claim, saying each literal 'is read back as the exact decimal it was written as', which holds for the specific short literals in that test and does not generalise. The associated aggregate_daily docstring line 128-130 is accurate as written and is not part of this finding.
likely_cause: A correct technical insight stated one step too strongly. The distinction between 'does not add error' and 'removes error already present' is easy to collapse when writing the comment that justifies the fix.
impact: A reader who takes the comment at face value concludes that float amounts are safe end to end and closes the ingestion question, which is the one remaining place where precision on this path can still be lost. For amounts at realistic transaction magnitudes the practical residual error is tiny, so the impact is on future decisions rather than on today's numbers: it removes the pressure to fix the ingestion boundary, which is the only fix that makes the exactness claim true.

fix.diff:
-    # Never Decimal(float): that would import the float's binary rounding
-    # error. Going through str preserves exactly the digits the caller gave.
+    # Never Decimal(float): that would expand the double's full binary value
+    # and import its rounding error into the total. str() yields the shortest
+    # decimal string that round-trips to the double we were handed, so this
+    # ADDS no error. It cannot REMOVE error: if the caller parsed decimal text
+    # into a float upstream, that precision is already gone and only a string
+    # or Decimal at the ingestion boundary can preserve it end to end.
fix.why: The replacement keeps the operative instruction (never Decimal(float)) and the reason for it, while stating the boundary of the guarantee explicitly. A reader now knows both that this line is correct and that the ingestion path is still an open question, which is the behaviour the comment should produce. The test docstring should be trimmed the same way, to claim only what it demonstrates: that these three specific literals round-trip and that a naive float accumulator would have crossed the limit while this one does not.

title: Test-code style: no correctness defect found in any of the 15 tests; the residual items are naming, import placement and an unmarked green test that asserts a regulatorily wrong outcome
standard: ruff --select ALL: I001 un-sorted import block, N802 function name should be lowercase, PLC0415 import should be at top level, D205 and D209 docstring formatting. The 16 S101 and 12 D103 hits in the same run are normal pytest idiom and are NOT raised. ruff's default profile passes both files with zero hits.
problem: Recorded primarily as a positive result, because Morgan asked specifically about test correctness. All 15 tests were traced by hand against the current source: every expected value is arithmetically right, including the two Decimal cases (0.1 + 0.2 + 9999.7 sums to exactly Decimal('10000.0') and is correctly asserted not reportable, while a naive float accumulator would reach 10000.000000000002 and report True, so the test genuinely discriminates); every pytest.raises match string is a substring of the message the corresponding raise actually produces, with no regex metacharacter problems; the exception types match (ValueError for the missing key, TypeError for the four type rejections); 'index 1' is correct for the second element in the two-record test; every import resolves to a symbol that exists, so nothing errors at collection; and the rebind test restores the module global in a finally block. Nothing asserts the wrong thing. The residual items are all style. ruff flags the un-sorted import block at line 11, the uppercase CR_02 in test_credit_nets_against_debit_CR_02_known_defect, the function-level import in the rebind test, and two docstring layout issues. One substantive style point: the CR-02 characterisation test is an ordinary passing green test whose assertions encode a regulatorily wrong outcome, and only its docstring says so. Separately, the rebind test mutates a module global, so it is not safe under pytest-xdist parallel execution even though it restores the value.
likely_cause: Ordinary style drift in a first test module written without the suite ever being run, which is exactly when import ordering and docstring layout go unchecked. The characterisation test's shape is a deliberate and defensible choice that simply lacks a machine-visible marker.
impact: No functional impact. The characterisation point has a small audit impact: a suite summary or a coverage report shows 15 passing tests, one of which certifies that a $15,000 cash deposit netted against a $6,000 withdrawal produces no alert. Anyone reading the summary rather than the docstring could take that as evidence the behaviour is approved. A marker makes the distinction visible without the docstring.

fix.diff:
-def test_credit_nets_against_debit_CR_02_known_defect() -> None:
+@pytest.mark.known_defect  # registered in pyproject: markers = ["known_defect: 
+                           # pins CURRENT WRONG behaviour, not desired behaviour"]
+def test_credit_nets_against_debit_cr02_known_defect() -> None:
...
-def test_runtime_rebind_of_daily_limit_takes_effect() -> None:
-    import alert_threshold_check as module
+import alert_threshold_check as module   # at top of file, with the others
+
+def test_runtime_rebind_of_daily_limit_takes_effect(monkeypatch) -> None:
+    monkeypatch.setattr(module, "DAILY_LIMIT", Decimal("500"))
fix.why: A registered marker makes the characterisation test's status visible to anyone reading a test report, not only to someone reading its docstring, and it lets CI list the pinned defects as a set. Lowercasing the id in the name clears N802 while keeping the cross-reference. monkeypatch.setattr does the rebind and restores it automatically, which removes the try/finally, removes the function-level import, and is safe under parallel execution. Run ruff --fix for I001, D209 and the FURB157 Decimal("10") hits. None of this changes what any test asserts.
